Neutrophil = "bacteria first"; Eosinophil = "E for allergy"; Monocyte = "macrophage, mop-up crew".

## Related topics
[[Blood Components and Normal Hematologic Values]], [[Chemotherapy Side Effects: Bone Marrow Suppression]], [[Aplastic Anemia]]

## Check against your textbook
Percent ranges for each white cell type are not in the handout; look them up in your book.

title: Schilling Test and Vitamin B12 Absorption Testing
body:
## What it is
A test used in pernicious anemia to find out whether the body absorbs vitamin B12. The client swallows a small amount of radioactive vitamin B12, and a 24-hour urine collection is done afterwards.

## Must-know facts
- Positive result: vitamin B12 is absent in the urine, meaning it was not absorbed (fits pernicious anemia, lack of intrinsic factor).
- Negative result: vitamin B12 is present in the urine, meaning it was absorbed.
- Why the urine? Absorbed B12 that the body does not need is excreted in urine; if it never gets absorbed, none appears.

## Assessment
Other diagnostic help in the handout: CBC and blood smear show low hemoglobin and hematocrit.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Explain the test and the need to collect all urine for the full 24 hours; a missed void spoils the result.
2. Label and store the container as directed; keep the client hydrated within limits.
3. Remember the client received a small radioactive dose; follow facility rules for handling urine.
4. After diagnosis, teach about lifelong B12 injections.

## How the exam asks about it
"A positive Schilling test means...?" Positive = abnormal = B12 absent in urine. The word "positive" misleads people who think it means the vitamin is present.

## Memory aid
Positive = problem = "Poor absorption, empty urine".

## Related topics
[[Pernicious Anemia (Vitamin B12 Deficiency)]], [[Anemias Compared: Cause, Key Sign and First Priority]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout test details are brief; many current textbooks stress B12 blood levels and antibody tests instead of the Schilling test. Check what your review book expects.

title: Routes of Chemotherapy Administration
body:
## What it is
Chemotherapy drugs can be put into the body in several ways, chosen to reach the tumor while limiting harm to normal tissue.

## Must-know facts
- Oral: the most convenient route.
- Intravenous: the most common route.
- Intramuscular.
- Intrathecal: into the fluid around the spinal cord and brain, often through an Ommaya reservoir (a small device placed under the scalp). Used when drug must reach the central nervous system.
- Intra-arterial: into the artery feeding the tumor.
- Intracavitary: into a body cavity.
- Intravesical: into the bladder (links to bladder cancer).
- Topical: on the skin (links to chemosurgery for skin lesions).
- Nitrosoureas cross the blood-brain barrier, which is why they are used for brain-related disease.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Verify the route in the order; confusing an IV and an intrathecal drug can be fatal. Why: some drugs are safe by one route only.
2. Follow safe-handling rules for every route: gloves, gown, face shield, hazardous labels.
3. For IV: check the vein for phlebitis and watch for extravasation (leakage into tissue).
4. For an Ommaya or other device: aseptic technique; watch for infection and headache.

## Complications and red flags
Pain, redness or swelling at an IV site during infusion (extravasation); fever or neck stiffness after intrathecal dosing (infection); bladder irritation after intravesical dosing.

## How the exam asks about it
"Which route is most common / most convenient?" IV and oral. "Which route delivers to the brain and spinal fluid?" Intrathecal.

## Related topics
[[Chemotherapy Drug Classes and Cell Cycle]], [[Safe Handling of Chemotherapy Drugs]], [[Bladder Cancer and Urinary Diversions]]

## Check against your textbook
Vesicant lists and extravasation management are not in the handout; learn them from your pharmacology text.

title: Urinary Diversion Surgeries Compared
body:
## What it is
After bladder removal or when the bladder cannot work, urine is rerouted. The handout lists nine surgeries in two groups.

## Must-know facts
- Stoma-forming surgeries (urine flows out to a pouch):
  - Ileal conduit: a piece of ileum is used as the stoma.
  - Ureterostomy: the ureters themselves are brought out as the stoma.
  - Vesicostomy: the bladder is used for the stoma.
  - Nephrostomy: a tube is placed into the kidney.
- Continent or bladder-replacement surgeries:
  - Ureterosigmoidostomy: the ureters are attached to the sigmoid colon (urine leaves with stool).
  - Neobladder: a new bladder made from bowel is joined to the urethra (the handout says ascending colon).
  - Kock pouch: ileum made into a pouch with a valve.
  - Indiana pouch: ascending colon used as the bladder.
  - Mitrofanoff: appendix and ileocecal valve used as the channel.

## Assessment
Painless hematuria is the earliest and most common bladder cancer sign; other findings: dysuria, hesitancy, pelvic or back pain.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Check the stoma color (pink to red, moist is healthy) and urine output; dark or dusky stoma needs immediate report. Why: poor blood supply means tissue death.
2. Give IV fluids and pain management as ordered.
3. Provide comfort measures and rest; teach pouch care and skin protection.
4. Support body-image concerns before and after surgery.

## Complications and red flags
Stoma necrosis, no urine for hours, infection signs, leakage, skin breakdown around the stoma.

## How the exam asks about it
Matching: surgery name to "what is used" (ileum, ureters, bladder, kidney, sigmoid, ascending colon, appendix).

## Memory aid
"Conduit = ileum; Indiana = ascending colon; Kock = valve; Mitrofanoff = appendix."

## Related topics
[[Bladder Cancer and Urinary Diversions]], [[Colostomy and Stoma Care]], [[Bowel Ostomies]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout's neobladder description (ascending colon to urethra) differs from many texts (usually ileum). The handout also says to decrease fluids; most texts encourage fluids. Verify both.

title: Colorectal Surgeries and Bowel Preparation
body:
## What it is
The operations used for colon and rectal cancer, and what the nurse does before and after.

## Must-know facts
- Hemicolectomy: removal of the right or left side of the colon.
- Transverse colectomy: removal of the transverse colon (the part that crosses from right to left).
- Sigmoidectomy: removal of the sigmoid colon.
- Miles' procedure: removes the tumor, part of the sigmoid, the whole rectum and the anal sphincter; a permanent colostomy results.

## Priority nursing actions
Before surgery (goal: a clean bowel to cut infection risk):
1. Low-residue diet for 3 to 5 days.
2. Clear liquids, then NPO after midnight.
3. Laxative and cleansing enema.
4. Neomycin tablet as the pre-op antibiotic (it reduces bowel bacteria).
After surgery:
1. Assess the stoma first: red and slightly protruding is normal; dusky, brown to black suggests necrosis, report at once.
2. Warm sitz bath for the perineal area.
3. Expect flatus and stool at about 4 to 7 days.
4. Protect skin (karaya paste, talc or cornstarch); never mineral oil.
5. Teach avoiding gas-forming foods.

## Complications and red flags
Bowel obstruction, hemorrhage, perforation, abscess, peritonitis, sepsis, shock.

## How the exam asks about it
Which operation causes a permanent colostomy (Miles); which pre-op measure is for infection (neomycin); which stoma finding is abnormal (dark or black).

## Related topics
[[Colorectal Cancer]], [[Colostomy and Stoma Care]], [[Preoperative Assessment and Patient Teaching]]

## Check against your textbook
Not every colorectal operation needs a stoma; the handout does not say which ones do. Pouch-emptying level and irrigation volumes differ between texts.

title: Preoperative Medications and Their Purpose
body:
## What it is
Drugs given before surgery to make anesthesia safer and the client calmer.

## Must-know facts
Goals listed in the handout:
- Reduce anxiety and promote relaxation.
- Reduce pharyngeal (throat) secretions.
- Prevent laryngospasm.
- Inhibit gastric secretion (lowers aspiration danger).
- Decrease the amount of anesthetic needed for induction and maintenance.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Give the premedication on time as ordered (it works only if given at the right time).
2. After the dose, keep the client in bed with side rails up. Why: drowsiness raises fall risk.
3. Confirm the signed consent is on the chart before sedating the client. Why: a sedated client cannot legally consent.
4. Verify NPO status, allergies, and that dentures, jewelry and valuables are handled.
5. Send the complete chart (checklist, consent, laboratory results) with the client.

## Complications and red flags
Excess drowsiness, slow breathing, hypotension, or confusion after the premedication.

## How the exam asks about it
"What is the purpose of a drying agent / sedative before surgery?" Reduce secretions; reduce anxiety. Another trap: the best time to get consent is before medication, not after.

## Related topics
[[General Anesthesia and Its Stages]], [[Immediate Pre-operative Preparation]], [[Informed Consent for Surgery]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout does not name the premedication drugs. Specific drugs and doses are for your pharmacology text.

title: PACU Airway and Circulation Management
body:
## What it is
The first priorities in the recovery room: keep the airway open, keep blood pressure and perfusion stable.

## Must-know facts
- Airway blockage by the tongue or secretions shows as choking, noisy, irregular breathing (hypopharyngeal obstruction).
- Hypotension after surgery can come from blood loss, hypoventilation, position change, blood pooling in the limbs, or drug and anesthetic effects.
- Shock after surgery commonly comes from low circulating volume (hypovolemia). The main treatment is volume replacement.
- Vital signs are checked every 15 minutes in the PACU (per handout).

## Assessment
Airway, breathing, circulation, skin color, level of consciousness, response to commands, surgical site drainage, tubes and lines.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Airway first: suction mucus or vomitus; take extra care after tonsil, mouth or laryngeal surgery. Why: no airway means no oxygen, and this outranks every other problem.
2. Give oxygen.
3. Check the incision and drains for bleeding.
4. Treat hypovolemia with fluids or blood as ordered; keep the client warm so normal temperature is maintained.
5. Monitor continuously until stable.

## Complications and red flags
Snoring, gurgling, stridor or silent chest; falling blood pressure with rapid weak pulse; restlessness; oliguria.

## How to reason about it
Cause -> finding -> action: low volume (cause) -> low BP, fast pulse, cold skin -> fluids/blood and find the bleeding. The trap: choosing pain medicine or paperwork before checking airway.

## Related topics
[[Post Anesthesia Care Unit and Aldrete Score]], [[Postoperative Hemorrhage and Hypovolemic Shock]], [[Management of Shock]]

## Check against your textbook
Positioning of the client in PACU is not stated in the handout; confirm side-lying versus other positions in your book.

title: Postoperative Pain and Nausea Control
body:
## What it is
Relieving pain and nausea right after surgery so the client can breathe deeply, move and heal.

## Must-know facts
- In the PACU, opioid pain relievers are mostly given IV because they act immediately and are short acting.
- Pain control also supports lung health: pain limits breathing, and uncontrolled pain leads to atelectasis.
- Act at the first mention of nausea, before vomiting starts. The handout names promethazine (Phenergan) and hydroxyzine (Atarax) as examples of drugs ordered to prevent postoperative nausea and vomiting.
- Deep breathing helps remove anesthetic from the body.
- Opioids can depress breathing; this is an important balancing act.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Monitor physiological status and pain level regularly.
2. Give analgesics as ordered, and use comfort measures and psychological support to ease fear.
3. Watch breathing rate and alertness after opioids. Why: respiratory depression is the main danger and takes priority over comfort.
4. Treat nausea at the first report; keep an emesis basin; turn the head to the side if vomiting to prevent aspiration.
5. Teach the client to ask for pain medicine early and to splint the incision.

## Complications and red flags
Slow or shallow breathing, hard to wake, vomiting in a drowsy client (aspiration), pain that is suddenly worse (bleeding, dehiscence).

## How the exam asks about it
"First action for a client who says 'I feel sick'?" Intervene at once (position, antiemetic as ordered), not wait for vomiting.

## Related topics
[[Post Anesthesia Care Unit and Aldrete Score]], [[Antiemetic Drugs]], [[Postoperative Respiratory Complications]]

## Check against your textbook
Pain scales and opioid doses are not in the handout; use your pharmacology text.

title: Postoperative Nutrition, Elimination and Fluid Balance
body:
## What it is
After surgery the body needs enough fluid, careful feeding and a working bowel. The handout lists these as priorities 4 and 6.

## Must-know facts
- Fluid and electrolytes: give enough fluid to maintain blood volume, but avoid overload, which causes pulmonary congestion and edema. Do not force fluids too soon.
- Keep accurate intake and output records and monitor serum electrolytes.
- Normal peristalsis returns in about 48 to 72 hours after surgery.
- Diet starts with liquids (broth, tea, juice, gelatin, soup) and is advanced as tolerated.
- Early ambulation helps prevent abdominal distention.

## Assessment
Bowel sounds, passing of flatus, abdominal distention, nausea, urine output, intake and output balance, breathing (for overload).

## Priority nursing actions
1. Record intake and output exactly. Why: low urine output is an early warning of low volume or kidney trouble.
2. Check bowel sounds and flatus before advancing the diet; start with liquids.
3. Encourage breathing exercises and walking.
4. Report distention, vomiting or absent flatus after expected return time.

## Complications and red flags
Fluid overload (crackles, shortness of breath, edema); dehydration (low urine, dry mucosa); distention and vomiting with no bowel activity.

## Related topics
[[Postoperative Priorities of Care]], [[Early Ambulation after Surgery]], [[Fluid Volume Excess (Hypervolemia)]], [[Fluid Volume Deficit (Hypovolemia)]]

## Check against your textbook
Post-abdominal-surgery nothing-by-mouth rules, nasogastric tube care and the term paralytic ileus are not in the handout; check your book.

title: Radiation Therapy Compared: External, Sealed and Unsealed
body:
## What it is
A comparison table in note form of the three radiation situations, since exam questions hinge on whether the client is radioactive.

## Must-know facts
- External (teletherapy): source far from the client; client NOT radioactive; no special isolation needed.
- Internal sealed (needles, seeds or beads, catheter, intracavitary): client IS radioactive; the source stays in place; body fluids NOT radioactive.
- Internal unsealed (IV or oral, e.g. iodine-131 for thyroid cancer): client IS radioactive; body fluids ARE radioactive.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Identify which type is in use. Why: the type decides how much protection staff and visitors need.
2. For internal radiation: shielding (lead gown, dosimeter badge), time (limit contact), distance (about 6 feet) and a private room.
3. Handout limits: 30 minutes per shift and 5 minutes per visit.
4. Never assign pregnant staff; no children as visitors.
5. Intracavitary: empty bladder and bowel, complete bed rest, low-residue diet, indwelling urinary catheter.
6. Unsealed: flush the toilet 3 times; visitors do not share the toilet.
7. External: protect the skin, no lotion or powder, leave markings, plan for fatigue.

## Complications and red flags
Radiodermatitis, severe fatigue, and for sealed implants, a dislodged source (do not touch with bare hands; follow policy).

## How to reason about it
The trap: assuming every radiation client is a hazard. Teletherapy = safe to touch. Sealed = body fluids are safe. Unsealed = all fluids are hot.

## Memory aid
Shielding, Time, Distance ("STD" in the handout).

## Related topics
[[External Radiation Therapy (Teletherapy)]], [[Internal Radiation Therapy (Brachytherapy) and Radiation Precautions]], [[Chemotherapy Drug Classes and Cell Cycle]]

## Check against your textbook
Time limits vary by policy and isotope; learn the handout numbers for the exam and confirm in your text.

title: Cancers of the Pancreas, Liver, Gallbladder, Colon, Bladder and Skin: Quick Comparison
body:
## What it is
One page that compares the six organ cancers in the handout: risk factors, key signs, diagnostic test and surgery.

## Must-know facts
- Pancreatic: smoking, diabetes, chronic pancreatitis, high-fat diet. Signs: abdominal pain, weight loss, clay-colored stools, blood sugar problems. Test: ERCP. Surgery: Whipple procedure.
- Hepatocellular (liver): hepatitis B, cirrhosis, aflatoxin, alcohol. Test: liver biopsy. Only cure: resection or transplant.
- Gallbladder: female, about age 65, gallstones. Tests: ultrasound, CT, ERCP. Surgery: cholecystectomy.
- Colorectal: age, polyps, family history, low-fiber high-fat diet. Signs: change in bowel habits (most common), blood in stool, pencil-like stool. Tests: digital rectal exam, fecal occult blood, colonoscopy, CEA. Surgery: hemicolectomy, Miles' procedure.
- Bladder: smoking, industrial chemicals, bladder stones. Sign: painless hematuria. Tests: cystoscopy, CT. Surgery: urinary diversions.
- Skin: sun exposure. Types: basal cell (most common), squamous cell (can spread), melanoma (deadliest). ABCDE rule. Treatment: electrosurgery, cryosurgery, radiation.

## How to reason about it
Match the "first sign" to the organ: painless hematuria -> bladder; clay stools and weight loss -> pancreas; change in bowel habit -> colon; changing mole -> melanoma. The trap is choosing a painful symptom for bladder cancer: its early sign is painless.

## Priority nursing actions
Across all six: pain control, fluids and nutrition, skin care (itching in pancreatic and bile duct problems), emotional support, and early reporting of complications.

## Related topics
[[Pancreatic Cancer and Whipple Procedure]], [[Hepatocellular Cancer]], [[Gallbladder Cancer and Post-Cholecystectomy Care]], [[Colorectal Cancer]], [[Bladder Cancer and Urinary Diversions]], [[Skin Cancer]]

## Check against your textbook
Summary built from the handout; some risk factors in the handout (insulin therapy, oral contraceptives for liver cancer) should be verified.

title: Drugs in Hematology and Oncology Nursing: Quick Reference
body:
## What it is
A list of every drug or drug group named in the three handouts, grouped by the problem it treats, so you can recall them together.

## Must-know facts
- Iron deficiency: ferrous sulfate, gluconate, fumarate (take with vitamin C, away from antacids and dairy).
- Pernicious anemia: vitamin B12 injections for life.
- Folic acid deficiency: folic acid 1 mg daily.
- Aplastic anemia: immunosuppressants, transfusions, antibiotics, antifungals; causative drugs to avoid include chloramphenicol and sulfonamides.
- Sickle cell: hydroxyurea.
- Polycythemia vera: hydroxyurea, anagrelide (inhibits platelet aggregation), interferon alfa-2b (itching; watch flu-like symptoms and depression), antihistamine, allopurinol (lowers uric acid).
- Hemophilia: factor VIII or IX concentrates, aminocaproic acid (blocks clot breakdown), desmopressin (temporary rise in factor VIII).
- Chemotherapy: antimetabolites, topoisomerase inhibitors, mitotic inhibitors, alkylating agents, antitumor antibiotics, nitrosoureas, hormonal agents, monoclonal antibodies.
- Chemotherapy support: antiemetics, erythropoietin (anemia), viscous lidocaine for mouth sores in adults (not children).
- Surgery: preoperative sedative or drying drugs, promethazine and hydroxyzine for nausea, opioids for pain.

## Priority nursing actions
Check the reason for each drug and the one safety rule that goes with it (route, interaction, or toxicity). Why: exam questions ask for the reason, not the dose.

## How the exam asks about it
"Which drug is correctly matched with its use?" or "Which instruction shows understanding of the drug?"

## Related topics
[[Chemotherapy Drug Classes and Cell Cycle]], [[Polycythemia Vera]], [[Hemophilia]], [[Sickle Cell Anemia and Crises]]

## Check against your textbook
No doses are given here other than those in the handout. Drug classes of hydroxyurea and other agents vary by book; confirm in your pharmacology text.
